newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat ends down on talk of private estimate.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat ends down on talk of private estimate.

text.p: CBOT wheat futures closed lower on talk that a closely followed private crop analyst estimated the weekend freeze loss in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat crop at only 50 million bushels, traders said.
There had been loss estimates from 50 million bushels to as much as 200 million bushels or more.
"The estimates are all over the place and they won't know for a week or two," a trader said, referring to the amount of wheat lost to the cold snap in the Plains.
But little if any damage occurred overnight Monday.
Meteorologists said temperatures overnight Monday did not reach levels which would cause further harm and it appears warmer temperatures are in store for much of the wheat growing region.
Two widely-followed analysts had sharply different views of the crop damage ranging from roughly 50 million bushels up to 200 million bushels, the traders said.
But profit taking was the key reason cited by many traders for the decline in futures Tuesday.
Wheat closed four to nine cents lower, with May down 7-1/4 at $4.15-3/4 per bushel.
Active new crop July moved in a 11-1/2 cent per bushel range and a higher opening quickly evaporated amid profit taking and sell stops.
"It was overdone. No one knows how much damage was out there," a trader said. "Once we got through (below) last night's close we hit sell stops."
Wheat rallied the 20-cent-per-bushel trading limit Monday and traded with expanded 30-cent limits Tuesday. The expanded limits remain in effect Wednesday.

But the market remained underpinned by concern about the extent of damage to the U.S. crop, prospects of delays in seeding of the U.S. spring wheat crop, dry weather in European production areas especially in France and dry weather in eastern Australian wheat growing areas.

USDA Monday said as of Sunday, 63 percent of the U.S. winter wheat crop was in good to excellent condition, versus 27 percent a year ago. Also two percent of the U.S. spring wheat crop had been planted as of Sunday, versus two percent a year ago and the seven-percent five-year average.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 25,000 contracts, above the 11,156 traded Monday.
Rosenthal Collins and Goldenberg Hehmeyer each sold two million bushels of July and Tenco Inc sold 2.3 million bushels of July, traders said.

In wheat options, Paine Webber bought 800 July $3.90 puts and sold 800 July $4.10 puts at 7-1/2 cents, traders said. Prudential Securities bought 450 September $4.30 calls at 30 cents and sold 450 September $4.50 calls at 16 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 20,000 contracts, below the 26,307 traded Monday.
